transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-04-18
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~42 minutes
Attendees: Maya Roberts (Redwood AE), Samir Patel (Redwood SE), Lena Ortiz (CTO - Harbor Finance), Avi Shah (Backend Lead), Morgan Lee (Security), Priya Desai (SWE)
Recording: auto-recorded

Summary:
Quick SDK integration walkthrough (Python + TypeScript), environment/auth setup, quickstarts and path to PoC. Discussed hosted vs dedicated for latency/cost, SSO/KMS questions from security. Agreed next steps to share pricing, security docs, and benchmark scripts.

Topics: SDK quickstart, API auth (API key vs token), env vars, example requests, streaming, embeddings, error handling, dedicated/vpc options, SOC2/KMS questions.

Transcript: 
[00:00] Maya: Hi everyone, thanks for taking the time, I'm Maya from Redwood Inference, AE on the account, with Samir our solutions engineer. How are you all doing?
[00:06] Lena: Doing well, thanks. Excited to see the SDK flow, we want something our engs can drop into services quickly.
[00:12] Samir: Awesome. Goal for today is to walk through the Python and TypeScript quickstarts, show auth, env setup, and a couple of tips for streaming and batching. We'll also answer security questions.
[00:22] Avi: High level — we're evaluating for customer-facing summarization. Latency needs to be under 400ms P95 for short prompts and cost is as big a factor.
[00:31] Maya: Great, note on latency/cost — we usually discuss hosted API for fast onboarding and dedicated pools if you need guaranteed throughput and lower unit cost. We'll show both options in the docs.
[00:40] Morgan: From security — we need to confirm KMS integration and audit logs, plus SSO for the console.
[00:45] Samir: Yep, we'll point you to the SOC2 and KMS docs, and the console supports SAML SSO and RBAC. I'll drop links after.

[00:58] Samir: Ok jumping into the Python quickstart — here's the typical flow. Set REDWOOD_API_KEY as env var, pip install redwood-sdk, then a couple of lines to call text generation.
[01:10] Samir (reading): "export REDWOOD_API_KEY=sk_live_XXX" — obviously use your real key and store in your secret manager. In Python:

  from redwood import RedwoodClient
  client = RedwoodClient(api_key=os.environ.get('REDWOOD_API_KEY'))
  resp = client.generate(model='redwood-1.3', prompt='Summarize this transaction...', max_tokens=120)
  print(resp.text)

[01:35] Priya: Quick question, does the Python SDK auto-retry and handle streaming?
[01:38] Samir: Good Q — yes, SDK has built-in retry/backoff and a streaming iterator API. Example:

  for chunk in client.stream_generate(...):
      print(chunk.partial)

Sometimes the transcription has "streaming iterator" turned into simpler words in the notes, but it's the standard approach.

[01:55] Lena: What's the preferred auth for Dedicated? We want to restrict keys to particular pools.
[02:00] Samir: For Dedicated you'll get tenant-scoped API keys plus optional short-lived tokens via your own identity provider. You can also mount KMS keys for encrypting model context at rest.

[02:20] Maya: I'll pause here — I noticed the team often uses environment injection or the cloud secret manager. Best practice is to set REDWOOD_API_KEY in your deploy pipeline secrets, and not commit to repo.

[02:30] Avi: For TypeScript quickstart?
[02:32] Samir: Yep, similar. npm install @redwood/inference or yarn add @redwood/inference, then in Node:

  import { Redwood } from '@redwood/inference';
  const client = new Redwood({ apiKey: process.env.REDWOOD_API_KEY });
  const out = await client.generate({ model: 'redwood-1.3', prompt: 'Extract merchant and amount from this text' });
  console.log(out.text);

[02:55] Priya: Any differences for edge runtimes or lambda?
[02:58] Samir: Use short-lived tokens for lambdas or edge. For long-running servers, use tenant keys. SDK supports both. Also recommend using the batching client for high-throughput async workers to amortize token cost.

[03:15] Lena: Can you show a quick error pattern? We have to map service errors to our retry logic.
[03:20] Samir: Sure — common statuses: 429 means throttle (backoff/retry), 503 is transient (retry), 401 is auth (rotate keys). SDK provides typed exceptions, but if you use raw HTTP you'll get JSON error body. Example in transcript sometimes mis-hears headers as "heders".

[03:36] Samir: I'll demo a small local run — I've got a quick example repo. (screen sharing noises) 
[03:45] [Screen share: repo structure - quickstart/python, quickstart/ts, examples/streaming, benchmarks/]
[03:52] Samir: Here's a sample .env.example:

  REDWOOD_API_KEY=sk_live_XXXX
  REDWOOD_API_URL=https://api.redwood.inference/v1

Note: the actual host is api.redwood.com in prod, docs show region variants like eu.api.redwood.inference for EU. Sometimes the transcriber turns that into "api redwood inference" in notes.

[04:15] Samir: Streaming example in TypeScript: you can listen to data events or use async iterators. For server-sent events you'll see chunks as they arrive.

[04:25] Maya: On the console side — quick note, you can create routes, pin model versions, enable caching policies and view token-level cost in the Console. We'll share screenshots.

[04:35] Lena: On caching — does Redwood do prefix caching across requests? We have repeated prompts with similar prefixes.
[04:40] Samir: Yes, KV cache/prefix caching is supported and can be enabled per-route. That reduces token usage for repetitive patterns. The runtime also handles KV cache invalidation on rollout.

[04:58] Morgan: Security — where are logs stored and for how long? We need audit logs for 1 year.
[05:03] Maya: We have configurable retention; enterprise plans can get longer retention and audit export. We also support pushing logs to your SIEM via an integration. I'll attach the security whitepaper.

[05:18] Avi: For our PoC we want to run a small benchmark: 200 concurrent users, short prompts, p95 < 400ms. How do we set that up?
[05:26] Samir: We'll provide a benchmark script and a recommended invocations-per-second pattern. For hosted, you might hit variability; Dedicated gives stable latency. I can share the exact benchmark config we used for a payments customer.

[05:40] Samir: Real quick, example of batching in Python — use the BatchedClient:

  from redwood import BatchedClient
  client = BatchedClient(api_key=os.environ['REDWOOD_API_KEY'], batch_size=8)
  responses = client.batch_generate(list_of_prompts)

This reduces per-token cost at the expense of a small queueing latency.

[06:05] Priya: Any notes on model selection and quantization? We are sensitive to memory footprint.
[06:09] Samir: We recommend smaller quantized variants for throughput; Redwood Optimize suggests profiles based on your workload (seq length, token count). We'll propose quantization and kernel choices in the recommendation doc.

[06:30] [Noise] Someone joined late.
[06:36] Maya: Welcome, we were just covering batching and SDK quickstarts.

[06:42] New voice (maybe recorded as Speaker 7): Hi, I'm Morgan, quick question on data residency — can you guarantee EU-only hosting for our EU customers?
[06:50] Samir: Yes, regioned deployments are available. For Hosted you can pick an EU region; for Private you can deploy on-prem. We'll include the region endpoints list.

[07:05] Lena: Regarding auth for PoC — can we create scoped keys? We don't want a key that can spin up Dedicated pools.
[07:10] Samir: Yes, scoped keys with least privilege are supported. Also short-lived tokens can be minted via your IDP for fine-grained access.

[07:22] Maya: I'll note to send the procedures for rotating keys and for restricting tokens.

[07:28] Priya: For our stack (Node backend + Python workers) how do you recommend organizing clients? Single shared pool or per-service keys?
[07:34] Samir: Typically per-service keys is safer — isolate blast radius. For cost tracking, route-level tags in the Console let you break down spend by service.

[07:48] Samir: I'm going to show a short live run — invoking the TS quickstart to show streaming. (bath of typing)

[08:00] [Demo: terminal output shows partial chunks, final text appears] 
[08:08] Samir: You can see partial chunks arriving, and then the final message. If your app needs low-latency tokens, use streaming to surface partial results to clients.

[08:18] Lena: Nice. Any caveats for mobile clients?
[08:22] Samir: Don't put API keys in the mobile app. Use a backend to proxy with short-lived tokens. It's a security anti-pattern otherwise.

[08:32] Morgan: For compliance we need to know where model inputs are stored and for how long.
[08:36] Maya: Inputs are retained per your plan; for Hosted short retention is default and you can opt-out or enforce no-retention. Dedicated/Private gives more control and you can set retention to zero. We'll attach retention SLA text.

[08:50] Avi: Ok let's talk timeline — we want to get PoC started next week and evaluate for Q2 production.
[08:56] Maya: Sounds good — typical PoC is 2-4 weeks, we'll agree on success criteria (p95 latency, accuracy on X test set, cost targets).

[09:06] Samir: I'm going to paste the quick links in chat now: quickstart repo, SDK README, benchmark script, security whitepaper. (link noise)

[09:14] Maya: I'll also send a tailored hosted vs dedicated cost estimate based on your target QPS.

[09:20] Priya: Quick follow — do you have a step-by-step for local dev to integrate with our CI?
[09:23] Samir: Yes, short checklist we recommend: set env vars in CI secrets, use short-lived tokens for ephemeral runners, run integration tests against sandbox endpoint, and gate usage with feature flags. We'll share the checklist.

[09:40] (Silence as Samir copies links)

[09:45] Samir: One more code tip — when you call embeddings for reranking, normalize vectors and use the embeddings client; the SDK exposes an embeddings() helper. Example:

  vec = client.embeddings(texts=[...])

Then store those in your nearest-neighbor index.

[09:58] Priya: Any rate limits we should expect on Hosted?
[10:02] Samir: Hosted has default rate limits per account but negotiable for enterprise. During PoC we can increase limits temporarily. 429s will happen if you exceed per-route limits.

[10:20] Lena: We're also evaluating Anthropic for safety features, any safety guardrails?
[10:25] Maya: Redwood has content filters and moderation hooks; for enterprise we can add custom filters or run additional post-processing. We can also route to a safer model variant automatically.

[10:40] Morgan: Let me ask about audit logs format — JSON lines preferred.
[10:44] Samir: We export logs as JSONL and also support pushing to your S3 or SIEM.

[10:52] Maya: Ok sounds like folks want links and docs. I'll summarize next steps.

Recap and next steps:
[11:00] Maya: 1) Maya to send pricing and Hosted vs Dedicated writeup + region endpoints (due 2026-04-20).
[11:06] Maya: 2) Samir to share benchmark config, quickstart repo, and example scripts (due 2026-04-21).
[11:12] Maya: 3) Harbor to confirm PoC goals/dataset (Lena to confirm by 2026-04-22).
[11:18] Maya: 4) Schedule PoC kickoff for week of 2026-04-26 (Maya will propose times).

[11:28] Lena: Thanks, this was helpful — the quickstart looks straightforward. We'll review the security docs and follow up.
[11:34] Maya: Great, we'll follow up in email with the attachments and links.

[11:40] (Meeting ends)

Notes about transcription: occasional mis-hearings — e.g., "KV cache" may appear as "KV cash" in auto transcription, and domain names often tokenized oddly. The recording captured screen share links and repo paths which are listed in the follow-up chat.
